title: Almond Flour vs Wheat Flour: Which Has Fewer Carbs?

seo.title: Almond Flour vs Wheat Flour: Carbs
seo.meta_description: Almond flour often has about 20–25 g total carbs per 100 g versus 75–77 g in refined wheat flour, but it contains far more fat and calories and behaves differently in baking.
seo.search_intent: Compare almond and wheat flour by carbs, fiber, fat, protein, calories, and baking behavior.

excerpt: Almond flour typically provides about 20–25 g of total carbohydrate per 100 g compared with roughly 75–77 g in refined wheat flour. It also contains much more fat and fiber, so it is not a lower-calorie or 1:1 baking substitute.
content_html:
Almond flour and wheat flour are not close in carbohydrate density. Almond flour often contains about 20–25 g of total carbohydrate per 100 g, including roughly 10–12 g fiber, while refined wheat flour is around 75–77 g carbohydrate with only about 2–4 g fiber.

Almond flour replaces starch with fat

Almond flour can exceed 50 g fat per 100 g, compared with roughly 1–2 g in refined wheat flour. That is why lower carbohydrate does not mean lower calorie: almond flour commonly reaches 570–620 calories per 100 g versus about 350–370 for wheat flour.

It has more protein but no gluten network

Almond flour may provide around 20–25 g protein per 100 g versus roughly 9–13 g in wheat flour. Those almond proteins do not form gluten, so the extra protein cannot replace wheat's structural role in bread.

A 1:1 baking swap usually fails

Almond flour brings fat, absorbs liquid differently, and lacks gluten. Cakes can become dense or oily and yeast breads lose the elastic network needed to trap gas.

Serving size changes the scale, not the pattern

Thirty grams is a more realistic baking portion than 100 g, but the same trade-off remains: fewer carbs, more fat, and a different structure.

Almond flour and wheat flour differ because they are made from fundamentally different parts of plants. Wheat flour is mostly ground cereal endosperm and is rich in starch, while almond flour is ground nuts and therefore contains much more fat, more fiber and far less starch. That is why almond flour is usually lower in available carbohydrate per gram, but it is also more calorie-dense. Calling one automatically 'healthier' misses the practical trade-off: they behave differently in recipes and fit different nutritional goals.

Protein numbers can also be misleading without context. Both can contribute protein, but wheat flour contains gluten-forming proteins that create elasticity and structure when mixed with water. Almond flour has no gluten, so it cannot build the same network. In bread, pizza or laminated dough, replacing wheat flour one-for-one with almond flour usually produces a dense or fragile result. Gluten-free recipes often combine almond flour with eggs, starches or other binders specifically to compensate for this structural difference rather than treating it as a direct flour swap.

Micronutrients and fats differ as well. Almond flour naturally brings vitamin E, magnesium and predominantly unsaturated fat, while enriched wheat flour may supply iron, folic acid and several B vitamins depending on the market and product. Whole-wheat flour adds more fiber and minerals than refined white flour. This means the comparison changes depending on which wheat flour you choose. A refined all-purpose flour, whole-wheat flour and almond flour are three distinct products, so a single carbohydrate number does not summarize their nutritional value.

For blood glucose or lower-carbohydrate cooking, almond flour can be useful because less of its weight comes from starch, but portion size still matters because it is energy-dense. For traditional baking, wheat flour is usually more predictable and economical. People with celiac disease need certified gluten-free ingredients and cannot use wheat flour; people with tree-nut allergy must avoid almond flour. Choose based on the recipe, dietary needs and total meal rather than assuming that a nut flour is automatically superior in every context.

The useful conclusion

Almond flour is much lower in total carbohydrate and higher in fiber, but it is more calorie-dense and cannot simply replace wheat flour cup for cup.

Almond flour and wheat flour also behave very differently in recipes. Almond flour brings more fat and moisture, so baked goods tend to be softer, denser, and more tender, while wheat flour develops gluten and gives breads and many cakes more stretch and structure. They are not reliable one-for-one substitutes in every recipe. Almond flour can be useful when you want fewer carbohydrates or need a gluten-free option, but it is more calorie-dense and may require different amounts of eggs, liquid, or leavening. Wheat flour remains the easier choice when a recipe depends on gluten for rise, chew, or shape.

faq.question: Which has fewer carbs?
faq.answer: Almond flour, roughly 20–25 g/100 g versus about 75–77 g/100 g in refined wheat flour.

faq.question: Does almond flour have fewer calories?
faq.answer: No. Its high fat content usually makes it more calorie-dense.

faq.question: Can it replace wheat flour 1:1?
faq.answer: Usually not. Almond flour lacks gluten and handles liquid very differently.
